idiom_name: public contract (interface or abstract class) with internal implementation plus factory/DI
implementation_notes: C# has no headers and assemblies ship metadata rather than source, so the compilation-firewall half of pimpl does not exist: private members and private nested types can change without forcing consumers to recompile, and adding members stays binary compatible. What remains - keeping the implementation type off the public surface - is expressed with the internal access modifier (assembly-scoped, and the default for top-level types), a public interface or abstract base as the contract, and a factory or DI registration that returns only the contract, while InternalsVisibleTo opens the implementation to test assemblies without publishing it. Write a pointer-to-impl wrapper only when the body is a native resource behind a P/Invoke handle, or when an object layout must stay fixed across a native boundary.
pitfalls: internal is per-assembly, not per-package: keep the implementation in the same assembly as the contract and a consumer can still reach it through reflection (or after InternalsVisibleTo), so the boundary is a packaging and API-review decision rather than a hard barrier.

Reflection-driven frameworks (DI scanning, serializers, mocking libraries) often need the concrete type, which pushes teams to make implementations public again; keep the composition root inside the implementation assembly so it can name the internal type.
Interface dispatch plus an extra layer is a real cost, so do not add the contract/implementation split for pure data classes or for objects created in tight loops.
